title: Why does this landscape look flood-carved?
subtitle: Channeled Scablands · Washington
deck: Eastern Washington is laced with empty channels too large for the creeks inside them. The scars are real — left by Ice Age floods from a vanished lake.
shortDescription: Glacial Lake Missoula outburst floods carved the coulees and dry cataracts of the Channeled Scablands.
seoTitle: What Carved the Channeled Scablands? Missoula Floods Explained — Deep Forest Dispatch
metaDescription: The Channeled Scablands were carved by repeated Ice Age floods from Glacial Lake Missoula — how to read coulees, Dry Falls, and flood-path evidence.

hero.alt: Landsat mosaic of eastern Washington showing flood-scoured Channeled Scablands channels in basalt
hero.credit: NASA Earth Observatory / Landsat + SRTM (Channeled Scablands)

blocks.html: From orbit, eastern Washington looks scratched — long coulees, basalt stripped bare, dry cataracts perched above tiny modern streams. The mismatch is the clue. Ordinary gradual erosion struggles to explain landforms this oversized.

blocks.alt: Schematic map from Glacial Lake Missoula through ice-dam failure into the Channeled Scablands and Columbia River system

sections.heading: A lake held by ice — then released

blocks.html: Near the end of the last Ice Age, the Cordilleran Ice Sheet dammed the Clark Fork River. Behind that ice dam, Glacial Lake Missoula grew in what is now western Montana — a volume NASA Earth Observatory compares to the combined waters of Lakes Erie and Ontario.

When the dam failed, floodwater tore southwest across the Columbia Plateau. The dam rebuilt and failed again — dozens of times over thousands of years, according to Ice Age Floods syntheses. Each pulse scoured basalt into channels, potholes, giant gravel bars, and current ripples at landscape scale.

blocks.caption: Eastern Washington — coulee country between Spokane and the Columbia.

blocks.alt: Detailed Landsat view of flood-scoured basalt channels in the Channeled Scablands
blocks.caption: Flood-scoured channels cut into Columbia River Basalt — farmable land stops where the flood stripped soil.
blocks.credit: NASA EO / Landsat 8 · Scars of Ice Age Floods · Public domain

blocks.html: Dry Falls is a scalloped cliff line — a cataract without water — hundreds of feet high and miles wide. In flood it was a waterfall of continental scale; today it is a dry signature you can stand beside. Coulees are the empty highways. Ripples and bars are the deposits.

J Harlen Bretz argued for catastrophic flooding when gradualism ruled geology. The landscape evidence — and Lake Missoula — eventually carried the case. This page is about the landforms, not a biography.
Satellites make the network obvious: anastomosing channels too wide for today’s creeks. Once you see the flood path, the scablands stop looking random.
